subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that x + y + 1 = 0 touches the circle x² + y² − 3x + 7y + 14 = 0 and find its point of contact.

mark_split.label: Set up the foot of the perpendicular
Solve for the point of contact

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, SENIOR INTER MATHS-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.51 — SAQ chapter 6 Circle, answer 48. The mark split 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 IS THE BOOK’S: this answer sits on a single-column page and carries printed margin tags — "1 Mark" beside the radius, "1 Mark" beside the line p = r, "1 Mark" beside the sentence naming the point of contact as the foot of the perpendicular, and "1 Mark" beside the values of h and k. It is the only printed split in the whole Circle SAQ chapter, and it is what the other SAQ splits in this unit are patterned on. Printed appearance tags: AP 17 and AP 22. Star rank: the book gives the CIRCLE SAQ chapter ★★ in its SAQ chapter table (book p.49), in the chapter header (book p.50) and in the SAQ hit list header (book p.9), so every Circle SAQ entry takes stars 2. That rank belongs to the CHAPTER, not to this question. Paper position: Maths-2B Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Circle holds Q11. Every number was re-derived and the book is correct: r = 1/√2 = p, and the point of contact is (2, −3). insider_note: Two separate things are asked and each carries two of the four marks — showing p = r, and then finding the point. Stopping after p = r loses half the marks.

steps.label: Radius of the circle
steps.margin_note: First printed mark, tagged "1 Mark" in the book. Both coefficients are odd, so keep everything over 4.
steps.memory_tip: g = −3/2 and f = 7/2. Square them as 9/4 and 49/4 and put 14 over 4 as well.
steps.why: A line touches a circle when its distance from the centre equals the radius, so the radius is needed before anything can be compared. Writing 14 as 56/4 keeps one denominator.
common_mistakes: Taking g = −3 and f = 7 without halving.

steps.label: Perpendicular distance equals the radius
steps.margin_note: Second printed mark, tagged "1 Mark". State p = r in words, not only as an equation.
steps.memory_tip: p = r means touching, p > r means the line misses, p < r means it cuts.
steps.why: A tangent meets a circle at exactly one point, and that happens exactly when the perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius. Both come out as 1/√2 here.
common_mistakes: Reaching p = r but not writing the sentence that the line touches the circle.

steps.label: Set up the foot of the perpendicular
steps.margin_note: Third printed mark, tagged "1 Mark". The sentence naming the point of contact as the foot of the perpendicular is what earns it.
steps.memory_tip: Point of contact = foot of the perpendicular from the centre to the tangent.
lines: The point of contact (h, k) is the foot of
steps.why: The radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent, so the point of contact is exactly where the perpendicular from the centre meets the line. That turns the geometry into the standard foot-of-perpendicular formula.
common_mistakes: Solving the line and the circle together, which works but is far longer.
Forgetting the minus sign in front of (ax₁ + by₁ + c).

steps.label: Solve for the point of contact
steps.margin_note: The last printed mark, tagged "1 Mark". Check the answer by putting it back into the line.
steps.memory_tip: Add 1/2 to each side of the two little equations and read h and k off.
steps.why: A quick check: 2 + (−3) + 1 = 0, so (2, −3) is on the line, and 4 + 9 − 6 − 21 + 14 = 0, so it is on the circle as well. A point on both is the point of contact.
common_mistakes: Writing k = 7/2 + 1/2 = 4 by using the wrong sign for the centre.
Reporting the centre as the point of contact.

steps.label: The picture
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own; the question does not ask for a diagram. The book prints one, and it shows why the radius is perpendicular to the tangent.
steps.memory_tip: The radius meets the tangent at right angles, so the contact point is the foot of that radius.

elements.text: p = r, so the line touches at P

steps.why: Because the tangent touches at a single point, the shortest distance from C to the line is the radius itself, drawn to that point. That single picture carries both halves of the question: p = r, and the contact point is the foot of the perpendicular.
common_mistakes: Drawing the line cutting the circle at two points.
Drawing the radius to a point other than where the line touches.
